The women, girded with a cord, sit down along the roads, burning bran as incense; 43. and when one of them, drawn aside by some passer-by, has lain with him, she reproaches her neighbor for not having been judged worthy of the same honor, and for not having had her cord of rushes broken. 44. Everything that is done regarding the idols is falsehood. How then can one believe or say that these are gods?</p>

<p class="v">45. They have been fashioned by craftsmen and goldsmiths; they can be nothing other than what the workmen intend them to be. 46. And the workmen who fashioned them do not have long to live: how then could their works be of long duration? 47. They have left nothing but falsehood and reproach to posterity. 48. Should a war arise, or some other calamity, the priests deliberate among themselves as to where they will hide with their gods: 49. how then can one fail to understand that these are not gods, which cannot save themselves from war or from any other calamity?</p>

<p class="v">50. These idols of wood, covered with gold and silver, will later be recognized as nothing but falsehood; to all the nations and to all the kings it will be evident that they are not gods, but works of the hands of men, and that there is in them no work of the divine. 51. To whom, then, would it not be evident that these are not gods?</p>

<p class="v">52. They will never set up a king over a land, nor will they give rain to men. 53. They will not know how to judge their own affairs, and they will not protect against injustice, since they can do nothing, being like crows that hover between heaven and earth. 54. And when fire falls upon the house of these gods of wood, covered with gold and silver, their priests will take flight and be saved; but the gods themselves will be consumed like beams in the midst of the flames. 55. They will withstand neither a king nor an enemy army. How then can one admit or think that these are gods?</p>

<p class="v">56. They will not escape thieves and robbers, these gods of wood, covered with silver and gold. 57. Men more powerful than they will carry off the silver and the gold, and go their way with the rich garments with which they were covered, and these gods will not be able to help themselves. 58. It is better, then, to be a king displaying his might, or a useful vessel in a house, one that its master uses, than to be these false gods; or even a door to a house, which guards what is within, than to be these false gods; or again a wooden pillar in the house of a king, than to be these false gods. 59. The sun, the light, and the stars, which are bright and sent for the benefit of men, obey God. 60. Likewise also the lightning, when it appears, is beautiful to see; the wind also blows over every land; 61. and the clouds, when God commands them to travel over all the earth, carry out what is ordered them. 62. Fire also, when it is sent from on high to consume the mountains and the forests, does what has been commanded it. But the idols are not to be compared, either in beauty or in power, to any of these things. 63. One must therefore neither think nor say that these are gods, since they can neither discern what is just, nor do good to men. 64. Knowing then that these are not gods, do not fear them.</p>

<p class="v">65. They are incapable of cursing or blessing kings. 66. They do not show the nations signs in the sky; they do not shine like the sun, they do not give light like the moon. 67. The beasts are worth more than they are, since by fleeing they can find shelter and be of use to themselves. 68. Thus in no way is it evident to us that these are gods; do not fear them, then.</p>

<p class="v">69. Just as a scarecrow in a field of cucumbers protects against nothing, so it is with their gods of wood, covered with gold and silver. 70. Wholly like a thornbush in a garden, on which every bird perches, or like a corpse thrown into a dark place, such are their gods of wood, covered with gold and silver. 71. The very purple and scarlet that decay upon them show that these are not gods. They themselves will in the end be devoured and become a disgrace in the land. 72. Better is the just man who has no idols; he will have nothing to fear from confusion.</p>

## Esther — The Greek Additions {: .book}

<p class="chap-sub">The dream of Mordecai, the prayers of Esther and Mordecai, the royal edicts — the chapters that the Hebrew Bible does not contain (Vulgate, ch. 10-16).</p>
### Chapter 10 {: .chap}

<p class="v">1. King Ahasuerus laid a tribute upon the mainland and the islands of the sea. 2. All the acts of his power and his exploits, and the full account of the greatness to which the king raised Mordecai, are these not written in the book of the Chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia? 3. For the Jew Mordecai was the king's chief minister, held in honor likewise among the Jews, beloved by the multitude of his brethren, seeking the good of his people and speaking for the happiness of his whole race.</p>

<p class="v">4. Then Mordecai said: "It is God who has done all these things! 5. For I remember the dream I had concerning this; not one detail of the vision has gone unfulfilled: 6. the little spring that became a river, and the light that arose, and the sun and the abundance of water. The river is Esther, whom the king took to wife and made queen. 7. The two dragons are myself and Haman. 8. The nations are those who gathered together to destroy the name of the Jews; 9. and my people is Israel, who cried out to God and was saved. Thus the Lord saved his people, and delivered us from all these evils; God worked miracles and great wonders, such as have never occurred among the nations. 10. To this end he prepared two lots: one for the people of God and one for all the nations. 11. And these two lots came at the hour, at the time, and on the day of judgment appointed before God for all the nations. 12. And God remembered his people, and did justice to his heritage. 13. And these days of the month of Adar, the fourteenth and the fifteenth of that month, shall be celebrated by them in assembly, with joy and gladness before God, throughout the generations, forever, in Israel, his people."</p>

### Chapter 11 {: .chap}

<p class="v">1. In the fourth year of the reign of Ptolemy and Cleopatra, Dositheus, who said he was a priest and of the race of Levi, together with Ptolemy his son, brought this letter of Phrourai, which they said was authentic and had been translated by Lysimachus, son of Ptolemy, residing at Jerusalem.</p>

<p class="v">2. In the second year of the reign of Ahasuerus the great king, on the first day of the month of Nisan, Mordecai, son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, of the tribe of Benjamin, had a dream. 3. He was a Jew who dwelt in the city of Susa, an illustrious man attached to the king's court. 4. He was among the number of the captives whom Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, had carried away from Jerusalem with Jeconiah, king of Judah.</p>

<p class="v">5. This was his dream: Suddenly voices were heard, a great noise and thunderings; the earth shook and was thrown into confusion. 6. Then suddenly two great dragons came forward, both ready for battle. 7. They let out a great cry, and at their voice all the nations made ready for the struggle, to fight against the people of the righteous. 8. Then suddenly it was a day of darkness and gloom; there was anguish, distress, tribulation, and great terror upon the earth. 9. The whole people of the righteous, fearing every evil for themselves, was in turmoil and preparing to perish. 10. They cried out to God, and at their cry there arose, as it were, a little spring, out of which came a great river, an abundance of water. 11. The light and the sun shone forth; those who were in humiliation were raised up, and they devoured those who were held in honor.</p>

<p class="v">12. Having awakened after seeing this dream and what God had resolved to do, Mordecai kept it engraved in his mind and, until nightfall, did all he could to understand it.</p>

### Chapter 12 {: .chap}

<p class="v">1. Now Mordecai remained at court with Bagathan and Thares, the king's two eunuchs, keepers of the palace gate. 2. Having learned their thoughts and penetrated their designs, he discovered that they had plotted to lay hands on King Ahasuerus, and he gave notice of it to the king. 3. The king had the two eunuchs put to the question, and, upon their confession, sent them to execution. 4. The king had what had happened written into the Chronicles, and Mordecai also set down a record of it in writing. 5. And the king ordered that he should hold an office in the palace, and gave him gifts for his denunciation. 6. But Haman, son of Hammedatha the Agagite, was in great honor with the king, and he sought to destroy Mordecai and his people on account of the king's two eunuchs.</p>

### Chapter 13 {: .chap}

<p class="v">1. Here is the copy of that letter:</p>

<p class="v">2. "Although I command a very great number of nations and have brought the whole world under my sway, I desire, not to abuse my power in order to grow proud, but, by a government ever clement and gentle, to secure continually for my subjects a life without disturbance; and, procuring for my kingdom calm and security to its farthest borders, to cause peace, dear to all mortals, to flourish anew. 3. Having therefore asked my counselors in what manner my intentions might be carried out, one of them, named Haman, who excels among us in wisdom, who is known for his unfailing devotion and constant fidelity, and who holds the second place in the kingdom, 4. made known to me that there is an ill-disposed people, mingled among all the tribes that are upon the earth, opposed to all peoples by reason of its laws, continually despising the commandments of kings, so as to hinder the perfect harmony of the empire we govern. 5. Having therefore learned that this people alone, in perpetual contradiction with all mankind, setting itself apart by the strange character of its laws, and ill-disposed toward our interests, commits the worst excesses and thereby hinders the prosperity of the kingdom, 6. we have ordered that those who are designated to you in the letters of Haman, who is at the head of affairs and honored as our second father, be all, with wives and children, utterly exterminated by the sword of their enemies, without any mercy or clemency, on the fourteenth day of the twelfth month, the month of Adar, of the present year; 7. so that these men, hostile formerly and still now, going down on the same day, by violent death, to the underworld, may restore to our affairs, for times to come, a perfect prosperity and peace."</p>

<p class="v">8. And Mordecai prayed to the Lord, remembering all his works. 9. He said:</p>

<p class="v">"Lord, Lord, almighty King, all things are subject to your power, and there is no one who can withstand you, if you have resolved to save Israel. 10. It is you who made heaven and earth, and all the wonders that are under heaven. 11. You are the Lord of all things, and none can resist you, O Lord! 12. You know all things, and you know that it was neither from insolence, nor from pride, nor from any desire for glory that I acted in not bowing down before the arrogant Haman, 13. for gladly, for the salvation of Israel, I would be ready to kiss the very tracks of his footsteps. 14. But I did it so as not to set the honor of a man above the honor due to my God; and never will I bow down before any other than you, my Lord, and it is not out of pride that I shall act so. 15. Now therefore, Lord my God and my King, God of Abraham, have pity on your people, because our enemies have cast their eyes upon us to destroy us and wish to destroy your ancient heritage. 16. Do not despise your portion, which you redeemed for yourself out of the land of Egypt. Hear my prayer! 17. Be favorable to your portion of inheritance and turn our mourning into joy, so that, our lives preserved, we may celebrate your name, Lord, and do not close the mouth of those who praise you."</p>

<p class="v">18. All Israel likewise cried out to the Lord with all their strength; for they had death before their eyes.</p>

### Chapter 14 {: .chap}

<p class="v">1. Queen Esther also, feeling herself placed in extreme peril of death, had recourse to the Lord. 2. Laying aside her splendid garments, she put on garments of anguish and mourning; in place of her precious perfumes, she covered her head with ashes and dust, harshly afflicted her body, and, tearing out her hair, filled with it all the places where she used to give herself over to joy. 3. And she addressed this prayer to the Lord, God of Israel:</p>

<p class="v">"My Lord, who alone are our King, assist me in my forsakenness, I who have no help but you; 4. for the danger that threatens me, I already feel it with my hands. 5. I learned from my earliest childhood, within my father's tribe, that you, Lord, chose Israel in preference to all nations, and our fathers in preference to all their ancestors, for your eternal heritage, and that you have fulfilled in their favor all your promises. 6. And now, we have sinned in your presence, and you have delivered us into the hands of our enemies, 7. because we paid homage to their gods. You are just, Lord! 8. And now, it is not enough for them to lay upon us a bitter servitude, but they have put their hands into the hands of their idols, 9. to swear an oath to abolish the decrees of your mouth, to destroy your heritage, to close the mouths of those who praise you, and to extinguish the glory of your temple and your altar, 10. so that the mouth of the nations may be opened, to praise the power of idols and to celebrate forever a king of flesh. 11. Do not deliver, Lord, your scepter to those who are nothing, lest they laugh at our ruin; but turn back upon them their own design, and make an example of the one who first raged against us. 12. Remember us, Lord; make yourself known in this time of our affliction, and give me courage, King of gods and Ruler of all power! 13. Put wise words upon my lips in the presence of the lion, and turn his heart to hatred of our enemy, that he may perish, he and all who share his sentiments. 14. But as for us, deliver us by your hand, and assist me, I who am alone and have none but you, Lord! You know all things, 15. and you know that I hate the splendor of the wicked, that I abhor the bed of the uncircumcised and of every stranger. 16. You know the constraint I am under, you know that I hold in horror the emblem of my exaltation that is set upon my head on the days I must show myself; I hold it in horror as a defiled cloth, and I do not wear it on the days I may spend in retirement. 17. Your servant has never eaten at Haman's table, nor made much of the king's feasts, nor drunk the wine of libations. 18. Never, from the day I was brought here until now, has your servant tasted joy, except in you, Lord God, God of Abraham. 19. O God, who surpass all in power, hear the prayer of those who have no other hope; deliver us from the hands of the wicked, and draw me out of my anguish!"</p>

### Chapter 15 {: .chap}

<p class="v">1. He sent word to Esther to come in to the king, in order to make supplication to him for her people and her homeland.</p>

<p class="v">2. "Remember," he said to her, "the days of your humble estate, and how you were nourished at my hand; for Haman, the first after the king, has spoken against us for our ruin. 3. But you, call upon the Lord, and speak for us to the king; save us from death!"</p>

<p class="v">4. On the third day, having finished her prayer, Esther laid aside her garments of penitence, and put on the ornaments of her dignity. 5. In the full splendor of her adornment, after having invoked God, the arbiter and savior of all, she took with her the two attendants she was accustomed to have. 6. She leaned upon one, as one scarcely able to support her delicate body; 7. the other followed, lifting up her mistress's long robe. 8. She herself, all flushed with the powerful radiance of her beauty, had a joyful countenance and an amiable air; but fear gripped her heart.</p>

<p class="v">9. Having thus passed through all the doors, she presented herself before the king. Ahasuerus was seated upon his royal throne, clothed with all the insignia of his majesty, all resplendent with gold and precious stones; his aspect was terrible. 10. When he had lifted up his head, radiant with glory, and cast a glance flashing with anger, the queen sank down in a faint, changing color and leaning upon the shoulder of the maidservant walking before her. 11. Then God changed the king's anger into gentleness; troubled, he sprang from his throne and held Esther in his arms, until she had recovered her senses, calming her fright with friendly words: 12. "What is it, Esther?" he said to her, "I am your brother, take courage; 13. you shall not die, for our decree is for our subjects in common. 14. Come near!" 15. And raising the golden scepter, he laid it upon her neck and gave her a kiss, saying: "Speak to me." 16. She answered: "I saw you, my lord, as an angel of God, and my heart was troubled by fear of your majesty; 17. for you are worthy of admiration, my lord, and your countenance is full of graciousness." 18. As she spoke, she sank down again, on the point of fainting. 19. The king was dismayed, and all his servants sought to revive the queen.</p>

### Chapter 16 {: .chap}

<p class="v">1. What follows is the copy of that letter:</p>

<p class="v">2. "Many, after having been heaped with distinctions by the great kindness of the princes their benefactors, become arrogant. 3. Not only do they take it upon themselves to oppress our subjects, but, unable to bear the weight of the honors, they weave plots against their own benefactors. 4. It is not enough for them to banish gratitude from among men; puffed up by the showy splendor of an unaccustomed fortune, they go so far as to persuade themselves that they will escape the avenging justice of God, who always sees all things. 5. Time and again, the crafty speech of men whom the friendship of princes had charged with administering affairs has engaged those who were at the head of empires in irremediable evils, making them accomplices in the shedding of innocent blood; 6. the deceitful lies of malice thus deceiving the benevolent simplicity of rulers. 7. And it is not only in ancient histories — as we have just recalled — that you may see impious deeds due to the pestilential influence of those who unworthily exercise power; you may see it even better by examining what happens close about you. 8. We must therefore provide for the future, so as to secure, in favor of all men, the tranquility and peace of the kingdom, 9. making the necessary changes and judging with prudence the matters that come before us, so as to meet them with constant fairness.</p>

<p class="v">10. "You know, indeed, how Haman, son of Hammedatha, a Macedonian, truly a stranger to the race of the Persians and far removed from our mildness, having been received by our hospitality, 11. experienced the effects of the benevolence we bear toward all peoples, to the point of being called our father and of seeing everyone prostrate themselves before him, as one holding the dignity nearest to the royal throne. 12. But, unable to bear so lofty a fortune with dignity, he set himself to deprive us of our kingship and our life. 13. By every sort of artifice and lies, he strove to destroy both Mordecai, who saved us and has always served us usefully, and Esther, the blameless companion of our royalty, together with their whole people. 14. In this way he hoped to surprise us in our isolation and hand over the empire of the Persians to the Macedonians. 15. But these Jews, doomed to death by the most villainous of men, we have found to be guilty of no fault, but rather to obey laws that are most just, 16. and to be the children of the Most High God, most great and eternally living, who, for us as for our ancestors, preserves this kingdom in the most flourishing state.</p>

<p class="v">17. "Wherefore you will do well to take no account of the letters sent by Haman, son of Hammedatha, 18. seeing that the author of these crimes has been hanged upon the gallows, with his whole household, before the gates of Susa; God, sovereign Master of all things, having inflicted upon him without delay the punishment he deserved. 19. Posting the copy of this present letter publicly in every place, allow the Jews to follow their laws in complete freedom, 20. and lend them assistance, so that they may repel the attack of those who, during the days of oppression, rose up against them; and this, on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, called Adar, on one and the same day. 21. For God, the Master of all things, has changed, for the chosen race, this day of misfortune into a day of gladness. 22. You, then, celebrate this great day also with every kind of rejoicing, as one of your solemn feasts, so that it may be, now and in time to come, 23. for us and for all who are well-disposed toward the Persians, a pledge of salvation, and, on the contrary, a reminder of ruin for those who plot against us.</p>

<p class="v">24. "Every city, and generally every region, that shall not have followed these directions shall be devastated with fury by sword and fire, so that it shall be forever, not only inaccessible to men, but abhorred even by wild beasts and birds.</p>

## The Additions to Daniel {: .book}

<p class="chap-sub">Three accounts transmitted through the Greek: the Song in the furnace, Susanna, Bel and the Dragon.</p>

### The Song of the Three Young Men {: .chap}

<p class="chap-sub">Daniel 3:24-90 — the prayer of Azariah and the song in the furnace</p>

<p class="v">24. And they walked about in the midst of the flame, praising God and blessing the Lord. 25. And Azariah, rising up, made this prayer; opening his mouth in the midst of the fire, he said:</p>

<p class="v">26. Blessed are you, Lord, God of our fathers;<br/>your name is worthy of praise and glory forever.<br/>27. For you are just in all that you have done to us,<br/>and all your works are true;<br/>your ways are right,<br/>and your judgments are equitable.<br/><br/>28. For you have rendered righteous judgments<br/>in all the evils that you have brought upon us;<br/>and upon the holy city of our fathers, Jerusalem;<br/>it is by a just judgment that you have done all this,<br/>because of our sins.<br/>29. For we have sinned and committed iniquity in withdrawing from you,<br/>and we have failed in all things.<br/>30. We have not listened to your commandments<br/>and we have not observed them,<br/>and we have not acted as you had commanded us,<br/>that we might be happy.<br/><br/>31. All that you have brought upon us,<br/>all that you have done to us,<br/>it is by a just judgment that you have done it.<br/>32. You have delivered us into the hands of unjust enemies,<br/>of apostates fiercely set against us,<br/>and of an unjust king, the most wicked in all the earth.<br/>33. And now we dare not open our mouths;<br/>shame and reproach belong to your servants,<br/>and to all who worship you.<br/><br/>34. Do not deliver us up forever, for the sake of your name,<br/>and do not destroy your covenant.<br/>35. Do not withdraw from us your mercy,<br/>for the sake of Abraham your friend,<br/>of Isaac your servant,<br/>and of Israel your holy one,<br/>36. to whom you promised to multiply their offspring<br/>like the stars of heaven,<br/>and like the sand that is on the seashore.</p>

<p class="v">37. For, Lord, we are brought low before all the nations,<br/>and we are today humbled throughout all your earth,<br/>because of our sins.<br/>38. There is no longer, at this time, for us,<br/>neither prince, nor leader, nor prophet,<br/>neither burnt offering, nor sacrifice, nor oblation, nor incense;<br/>nor a place to bring before you the firstfruits and find favor.<br/><br/>39. But, Lord, may we be received,<br/>with a contrite heart and a humbled spirit,<br/>40. as you receive a burnt offering of rams and bulls,<br/>or of a thousand fat lambs;<br/>so let our sacrifice be before you today,<br/>and our submission to you,<br/>for there is no confusion for those who trust in you.<br/>41. Now we follow you with all our heart,<br/>we fear you and we seek your face.<br/><br/>42. Do not put us to confusion,<br/>but deal with us according to your gentleness,<br/>and according to the abundance of your mercy.<br/>43. Deliver us by your wonders,<br/>and give glory, Lord, to your name.<br/>44. Let all who mistreat your servants be confounded,<br/>covered with shame by the loss of all their power,<br/>and let their strength be broken,<br/>45. let them know that you are the Lord, the only God,<br/>and the glorious sovereign of all the earth!"</p>

<p class="v">46. Meanwhile the king's servants who had cast these three men into the furnace did not cease to heat it with naphtha, tow, pitch, and brushwood. 47. The flame rose forty-nine cubits above the furnace; 48. and, bursting forth, it burned the Chaldeans it met near the furnace.</p>

<p class="v">49. But the angel of the Lord had come down into the furnace with Azariah and his companions, and he drove the flame of fire away from the furnace. 50. And he made the midst of the furnace as though a wind of dew had blown through it; and the fire did not even touch them, it did not injure them nor cause them the slightest harm.</p>

<p class="v">51. Then these three men, as with one mouth, praised, glorified, and blessed God in the furnace, saying:</p>

<p class="v">52. You are blessed, Lord, God of our fathers,<br/>worthy to be praised, glorified, and exalted forever.<br/>Blessed is your holy and glorious name,<br/>worthy of supreme praise and exaltation forever and ever.<br/>53. You are blessed in the temple of your holy glory,<br/>worthy of supreme praise and glory forever.<br/>54. You are blessed on the throne of your kingdom,<br/>worthy of supreme praise and exaltation forever.<br/>55. You are blessed, you whose gaze penetrates the depths,<br/>and who are seated upon the Cherubim,<br/>worthy of supreme praise and exaltation forever.<br/>56. You are blessed in the firmament of heaven,<br/>worthy of praise and glory forever.<br/><br/>57. Bless the Lord, all you works of the Lord;<br/>praise him and exalt him forever.<br/>58. Angels of the Lord, bless the Lord;<br/>praise him and exalt him forever.</p>

<p class="v">59. Heavens, bless the Lord;<br/>praise him and exalt him forever.<br/>60. Waters, and all that is above the heavens, bless the Lord;<br/>praise him and exalt him forever.<br/>61. Powers of the Lord, bless the Lord, all of you;<br/>praise him and exalt him forever.<br/><br/>62. Sun and moon, bless the Lord;<br/>praise him and exalt him forever.<br/>63. Stars of heaven, bless the Lord;<br/>praise him and exalt him forever.<br/>64. Every shower and dew, bless the Lord, all of you;<br/>praise him and exalt him forever.<br/>65. Winds that God lets loose, bless the Lord, all of you;<br/>praise him and exalt him forever.<br/><br/>66. Fire and heat, bless the Lord;<br/>praise him and exalt him forever.<br/>67. Cold and heat, bless the Lord;<br/>praise him and exalt him forever.<br/>68. Dews and frosts, bless the Lord;<br/>praise him and exalt him forever.<br/>69. Frost and cold, bless the Lord;<br/>praise him and exalt him forever.<br/>70. Ice and snow, bless the Lord;<br/>praise him and exalt him forever.<br/><br/>71. Nights and days, bless the Lord;<br/>praise him and exalt him forever.<br/>72. Light and darkness, bless the Lord;<br/>praise him and exalt him forever.<br/>73. Lightnings and dark clouds, bless the Lord;<br/>praise him and exalt him forever.<br/>74. Let the earth bless the Lord;<br/>let it praise him and exalt him forever!<br/><br/>75. Mountains and hills, bless the Lord;<br/>praise him and exalt him forever.<br/>76. Plants that grow upon the earth, bless the Lord, all of you;<br/>praise him and exalt him forever.<br/>77. Fountains, bless the Lord;<br/>praise him and exalt him forever.<br/>78. Seas and rivers, bless the Lord;<br/>praise him and exalt him forever.<br/><br/>79. Sea monsters and all that stirs in the waters, bless the Lord;<br/>praise him and exalt him forever.<br/>80. Birds of the air, bless the Lord, all of you;<br/>praise him and exalt him forever.<br/>81. Wild beasts and cattle, bless the Lord, all of you;<br/>praise him and exalt him forever.<br/>82. Children of men, bless the Lord;<br/>praise him and exalt him forever.<br/>83. Let Israel bless the Lord;<br/>let it praise him and exalt him forever!<br/><br/>84. Priests of the Lord, bless the Lord;<br/>praise him and exalt him forever.<br/>85. Servants of the Lord, bless the Lord;<br/>praise him and exalt him forever.<br/>86. Spirits and souls of the righteous, bless the Lord;<br/>praise him and exalt him forever.</p>

<p class="v">87. Saints and humble of heart, bless the Lord;<br/>praise him and exalt him forever.<br/>88. Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael, bless the Lord;<br/>praise him and exalt him forever.<br/><br/>For he has drawn us out of Sheol,<br/>and delivered us from the power of death;<br/>he has saved us from the midst of the burning flame,<br/>and drawn us out from the midst of the fire.<br/>89. Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good,<br/>for his mercy endures forever.<br/>90. All you godly men,<br/>bless the Lord, the God of gods;<br/>praise him and give thanks to him,<br/>for his mercy endures forever.</p>

### The Story of Susanna {: .chap}

<p class="chap-sub">Daniel 13 — "God stirred up the holy spirit of a young child named Daniel"</p>

<p class="v">1. There was a man dwelling in Babylon, whose name was Joakim. 2. He took a wife named Susanna, daughter of Hilkiah, of great beauty and fearing God; 3. for her parents, who were righteous, had instructed their daughter according to the law of Moses. 4. Now Joakim was very rich, and he had a garden near his house, and the Jews flocked to him, because he was the most honorable of all.</p>

<p class="v">5. That year two elders from among the people had been appointed judges, of whom the Master has said: "Iniquity came forth from Babylon, from elders who were judges, who seemed to govern the people." 6. They frequented the house of Joakim, and all who had disputes came to them. 7. About the middle of the day, when the people had withdrawn, Susanna would go into her husband's garden and walk there. 8. The two elders saw her go in and walk there every day, and they conceived a burning passion for her. 9. They perverted their minds and turned away their eyes, so as not to look toward heaven and not to remember the righteous judgments of God. 10. They were therefore wounded with love for her, but they did not confide their suffering to one another, 11. for they were ashamed to reveal to each other the passion that made them desire to be with her. 12. They watched for her carefully every day to see her, and they said to one another: 13. "Let us go home, it is dinner time." And they went out and parted from each other. 14. But having retraced their steps, they met one another, and having asked each other the reason for their return, they confessed their passion to each other; then they agreed between themselves upon the moment when they might find her alone.</p>

<p class="v">15. As they were watching for a suitable day, it happened that Susanna went into the garden, as she had done the day before and the day before that, with no company but two young maidservants; she wished to bathe in the garden, for it was hot. 16. There was no one there but the two elders, who had hidden themselves and were watching her. 17. She said to the maidservants: "Bring me perfumed oil and ointments, and shut the garden doors, so that I may bathe." 18. They did as Susanna had commanded and, having shut the garden door, went out by a back door, to fetch what had been asked of them; they did not know that the elders were hidden in the garden.</p>

<p class="v">19. As soon as the maidservants had gone out, the two elders rose up, ran to Susanna, and said to her: 20. "See, the garden doors are shut, no one can see us, and we are burning with love for you; consent, then, to our desire and be ours. 21. If not, we will bear witness against you, and we will say that a young man was with you, and that this is why you sent away the maidservants." 22. Susanna sighed and said: "On every side anguish surrounds me. If I do this, it is death for me, and if I do not do it, I will not escape from your hands. 23. But it is better for me to fall into your hands without having done wrong than to sin in the presence of the Lord." 24. Then Susanna cried out with a loud voice, and the two elders cried out also against her. 25. And one of them ran to open the garden doors. 26. When the servants of the house heard the outcry raised in the garden, they rushed in by the back door to see what was happening. 27. When the elders had told their story, the servants were greatly ashamed, for nothing like this had ever been said of Susanna.</p>

<p class="v">28. The next day, the people having gathered at the house of Joakim, Susanna's husband, the two elders came there also, full of wicked thoughts against her, in order to bring about her death. 29. They said before the people: "Send for Susanna, daughter of Hilkiah, wife of Joakim." And they sent at once. 30. She came with her parents, her children, and all her relatives. 31. Now Susanna had delicate features and great beauty. 32. As she was veiled, the wicked judges commanded that her veil be removed, that they might feast their eyes on her beauty. 33. But all her people and all who knew her wept. 34. The two elders, rising up in the midst of the people, laid their hands upon her head. 35. She, weeping, looked up toward heaven, for her heart trusted in the Lord. 36. The elders said: "As we were walking alone in the garden, she came in with two maidservants and, having had the garden doors shut, sent the maidservants away. 37. And a young man who was hidden came to her and did wrong with her. 38. We were in a corner of the garden; seeing the crime, we ran to them, and we saw them in this shameful act. 39. We could not seize the young man, because he was stronger than we were, and, having opened the door, he escaped. 40. But as for her, after we had seized her, we asked her who this young man was, and she would not tell us. This is what we attest." 41. The crowd believed them, because they were elders and judges of the people, and they condemned her to death.</p>

<p class="v">42. Then Susanna cried out with a loud voice and said: "Eternal God, who know what is hidden and who know all things before they come to pass, 43. you know that they have borne false witness against me; and here I am about to die, without having done any of what they have wickedly invented against me." 44. The Lord heard her voice. 45. As she was being led to death, God stirred up the holy spirit of a young child named Daniel. 46. He cried out with a loud voice: "As for me, I am innocent of this woman's blood!" 47. All the people turned toward him and said to him: "What do you mean by these words you have just spoken?" 48. Daniel, standing in the midst of them, said: "Are you then so foolish, children of Israel, as to put a daughter of Israel to death without examination, without seeking to know the truth? 49. Return to the tribunal, for they have borne false witness against her."</p>

<p class="v">50. Then the people returned in haste, and the elders said to Daniel: 51. "Come, take your place among us, and set forth your judgment to us, for God has given you the honor of old age." Daniel said to the people: "Separate them far from one another, and I will judge them." 52. When they had been separated from one another, Daniel called one of them and said to him: "You who have grown old in wickedness, the sins you committed in the past have now come upon you,</p>

<p class="v">53. you who used to give unjust judgments, who condemned the innocent and released the guilty, when the Lord has said: You shall not put to death the innocent and the righteous. 54. Well then, if you saw her, tell me under what tree you saw them talking together." He answered: "Under a mastic tree."</p>

<p class="v">55. Daniel said: "Just so, you have told a lie to your own destruction; for the angel of God, who has already received the divine sentence, is about to split you in two." 56. Having sent him away, he ordered the other to be brought, and said to him: "Offspring of Canaan, and not of Judah, the beauty of a woman has seduced you, and passion has perverted your heart. 57. This is how you used to deal with the daughters of Israel, and they, fearing you, would speak with you; but a daughter of Judah could not endure your wickedness. 58. Tell me, then, now, under what tree you caught them talking together." 59. He said: "Under an oak." Daniel said to him: "Just so, you too have told a lie to your own destruction; for the angel of the Lord waits, sword in hand, for the moment to cut you in two, in order to put you both to death."</p>

<p class="v">60. Then the whole assembly cried out with a loud voice, and they blessed God, who saves those who hope in him. 61. Then they rose up against the two elders, whom Daniel had convicted, out of their own mouths, of having borne false witness, and they did to them the harm that they themselves had wished to do to their neighbor; 62. thus fulfilling the law of Moses, and they put them to death, and innocent blood was saved that day. 63. Hilkiah and his wife praised God concerning their daughter Susanna, together with Joakim her husband and all her relatives, because nothing dishonorable had been found in her. 64. And Daniel became great in the eyes of the people, from that day onward and for the times to come.</p>

### Bel and the Dragon {: .chap}

<p class="chap-sub">Daniel 14 — the idols exposed, Daniel in the lions' den</p>

<p class="v">65. King Astyages having been gathered to his fathers, Cyrus the Persian received the kingdom.</p>

<p class="v">1. Now Daniel ate at the king's table, and he was honored above all the king's other friends.</p>

<p class="v">2. The Babylonians had an idol named Bel; every day there were spent upon it twelve measures of fine flour, forty sheep, and six vessels of wine. 3. The king also revered it, and went every day to worship it; but Daniel worshiped his own God. 4. The king said to him: "Why do you not worship Bel?" He answered him: "Because I do not revere idols made by human hands, but the living God, who made heaven and earth and has power over all flesh." 5. The king said to him: "Does Bel not seem to you to be a living being? Do you not see all that he eats and drinks every day?" 6. Daniel answered, smiling: "Do not be deceived, O king; for he is clay within and bronze without, and he has never eaten anything." 7. The king, angered, called the priests of Bel and said to them: "If you do not tell me who it is that eats these offerings, you shall die; 8. but if you show me that it is Bel who eats them, Daniel shall die, because he has blasphemed against Bel."</p>

<p class="v">9. Now there were seventy priests of Bel, not counting their wives and children. And the king went with Daniel to the temple of Bel. 10. The priests of Bel said: "See, we are going to go out; you, O king, have the food set out and the wine brought, after mixing it; then shut the door, and seal it with your ring. 11. And when you come in tomorrow morning, if you do not find that everything has been eaten by Bel, we shall die; or else it shall be Daniel, who has lied against us all." 12. They were confident, for they had made a secret opening under the table, through which they always let themselves in and came to consume the offerings.</p>

<p class="v">13. When they had gone out and the king had had the food placed before Bel, Daniel commanded his servants to bring ashes, and they scattered them throughout the whole temple in the presence of the king alone; then they went out, shut the door, sealing it with the king's ring, and departed. 14. During the night, the priests came in as was their custom, with their wives and children, and they ate and drank all that was there.</p>

<p class="v">15. The king rose at daybreak, and Daniel with him. 16. The king said: "Are the seals intact, Daniel?" He answered: "They are intact, O king." 17. As soon as he had opened the door and looked at the table, the king cried out with a loud voice: "You are great, O Bel, and there is not the slightest deceit in you." 18. Daniel began to laugh and, holding the king back so that he should not go in any farther, said to him: "Look at the pavement, and consider whose footprints these are." 19. The king said: "I see the footprints of men, women, and children"; and the king was filled with great anger. 20. Then he had the priests seized, together with their wives and children, and they showed him the secret doors through which they used to let themselves in and come to eat what was on the table. 21. He put them to death and handed Bel over to the power of Daniel, who destroyed it along with its temple.</p>

<p class="v">22. There was also a great dragon, and the Babylonians revered it. 23. The king said to Daniel: "Will you say again that this one is bronze? See, it lives, it eats and drinks. Now you cannot say that this is not a living god." 24. Daniel answered: "I worship the Lord my God, for he is a living God; but this one is not a living god at all. 25. You, O king, give me permission, and I will kill this dragon without sword or club." 26. The king said: "I give it to you." Then Daniel took pitch, fat, and hair, boiled them all together, and made them into cakes, which he threw into the dragon's mouth. And the dragon burst asunder. And he said: "See what you were revering!"</p>

<p class="v">27. The Babylonians, having learned of this, were seized with fierce indignation; they gathered together against the king and said: "The king has become a Jew; he has destroyed Bel, killed the dragon, and put the priests to death." 28. So they came to the king and said to him: "Hand Daniel over to us; otherwise we will put you to death, you and your household." 29. The king saw that they were falling upon him with violence; yielding to necessity, he handed Daniel over to them. 30. They threw him into the lions' den, and he remained there six days. 31. In the den there were seven lions, and they were given two corpses and two sheep every day; but then this food was withheld from them, so that they would devour Daniel.</p>

<p class="v">32. Now the prophet Habakkuk was in Judea; having cooked a pottage and crumbled bread into a vessel, he was going to the fields to bring it to his reapers. 33. The angel of the Lord said to Habakkuk: "Take the meal you are carrying to Babylon, to Daniel, who is in the lions' den." 34. Habakkuk said: "Lord, I have never seen Babylon, and I do not know the den." 35. Then the angel took him by the crown of the head, carried him by the hair of his head, and set him down at Babylon, above the den, with all the swiftness of his spiritual nature. 36. And Habakkuk cried out: "Daniel, servant of God, take the meal that God sends you." 37. Daniel answered: "You have indeed remembered me, O God, and you have not abandoned those who love you." 38. And Daniel rose up and ate. And the angel of the Lord immediately set Habakkuk back in his own place.</p>

<p class="v">39. On the seventh day, the king came to mourn for Daniel; having come to the den, he looked, and behold, Daniel was sitting in the midst of the lions. 40. He cried out with a loud voice and said: "You are great, Lord, God of Daniel, and there is none other than you!" And he drew him out of the lions' den. 41. Then he had those who had sought his destruction thrown into the den, and they were devoured before his eyes, in an instant. 42. Then the king said: "Let all the inhabitants of the whole earth fear the God of Daniel, for he is the Savior, who works signs and wonders on earth, he who delivered Daniel from the lions' den!"</p>

# Part Six <SEP> The Books Never Translated into French

<p class="part-sub">Notices on the writings of the Ethiopian canon that have never been translated into French</p>

The books presented here are fully canonical in Ethiopia, but no French translation of them has ever
been published — for some, the only modern (English) translations date from the 2010s and remain under
copyright. These notices give the essentials: what they are, what they recount, what they teach.

## 1 Meqabyan — The First Book of the Ethiopian Maccabees {: .noticetitle}

<p class="geez">36 chapters · composed in Ge'ez · unrelated to the Greek Maccabees</p>

Despite their name, the three <i>Meqabyan</i> do not recount the revolt of Judas Maccabeus: they are
books unique to Ethiopia, probably composed directly in Ge'ez in the Middle Ages from older traditions,
and carried by one shared conviction: the resurrection of the dead and the judgment.

The first book opens with the figure of a persecuting pagan king, Tsirutsaydan, a symbol of the pride
of the powerful. Arrayed against him stand brothers descended from Benjamin — the "Maccabees" of the
title — who refuse to worship idols. Arrested, and ordered to renounce the God of Israel, they confess
their faith and die as martyrs in the flames. Their martyrdom occupies the first part of the book; what
follows is a long prophetic meditation: God avenges the blood of the righteous, empires pass away, bodies
will rise again. The book develops, with an insistence rare in ancient literature, the doctrine of the
<b>resurrection of the dead</b> — one of the reasons for its authority in Ethiopia.

It also contains retellings of biblical history: the fall of Adam, the flood, Sennacherib and
Nebuchadnezzar summoned as figures of chastised pride, and the announcement that the Creator will not
leave his people without a defender.

## 2 Meqabyan — The Second Book of the Ethiopian Maccabees {: .noticetitle}

<p class="geez">21 chapters · a sermon on repentance</p>

The second book first takes up the thread of the first: King Meqabis, at first an enemy of Israel,
marches against Jerusalem; but struck by the word of a prophet, he is converted, and becomes a preacher
of repentance — a spectacular reversal that sets the tone for the whole book. What follows broadens the
meditation: what does it profit a man to rule if he loses his soul? The chapters review the famous
sinners and penitents of sacred history, and culminate in an appeal: God does not desire the death of
the sinner, but that he be converted and live.

The theology is simple and powerful: judgment is certain, mercy is real, and repentance is possible
until the last breath. Several passages foretell the resurrection and the retribution, echoing the
first book.

## 3 Meqabyan — The Third Book of the Ethiopian Maccabees {: .noticetitle}

<p class="geez">10 chapters · a homily on the salvation of the righteous</p>

The shortest of the three is a continuous homily, without a framing narrative: it contemplates the
salvation of the righteous and the ruin of the wicked through the great biblical figures — Adam saved
after the fall, Job tested and restored, David a sinner and forgiven, Elijah taken up. The thread
running through it: God never abandons those who hope in him; he chastises, but in order to bring
back; and in the end, he will raise up his own. The book ends in a doxology, in a movement close to
the great Ethiopian liturgical anaphoras.

## Josippon — The History of the Jews {: .noticetitle}

<p class="geez">Zëna Ayhud, "the Account of the Jews" · Ge'ez adaptation (14th c.) of a 10th-century Hebrew chronicle</p>

The <i>Zëna Ayhud</i> is the Ethiopian version of <b>Josippon</b>, a chronicle composed in Hebrew in
southern Italy around the 10th century, drawing on Flavius Josephus, and carried over into Ge'ez by way
of an Arabic version. It recounts the history of the Jewish people from the table of nations down to the
catastrophe of the year 70: Alexander the Great, the Maccabees (the real ones, this time), Herod, the war
against Rome, and the destruction of the Temple by Titus — a narrative that Ethiopia reads as the
fulfillment of prophetic warnings. It is, within the expanded canon, the "history" book par excellence;
among the Ethiopians it holds the place that 1-2 Maccabees hold among Catholics.

## The Expanded New Testament: Sinodos, the Book of the Covenant, Clement, the Didascalia {: .noticetitle}

<p class="geez">Eight books that bring the Ethiopian New Testament from 27 to 35 writings</p>

The "expanded" canon of the Ethiopian New Testament adds eight books of an ecclesiastical order — not
additional gospels, but the law and liturgy that the Ethiopian Church holds to have been inherited from
the apostles:

<b>The Sinodos</b> (four books: Ser'atä Seyon, Te'ezaz, Gessew, Abtelis) — a great collection of canons
attributed to the apostles gathered in council: the ordination of bishops, priests, and deacons, the
discipline of the faithful, prayers of thanksgiving. It incorporates very ancient materials, related to
the <i>Apostolic Tradition</i> and the <i>Canons of the Apostles</i> known elsewhere in Greek and Latin.

<b>The Book of the Covenant</b> (Mäshafä Kidan, in two parts) — the first regulates divine worship; the
second, related to the <i>Testament of Our Lord</i>, gives a discourse of the risen Christ to his
disciples on the last times and the order of the Church.

<b>The Ethiopian Clement</b> (Qälëmentos, seven books) — revelations that Peter is said to have entrusted
to Clement of Rome: sacred history from Adam onward, precepts, an apocalypse. Distinct from the letters
of Clement known in Greek.

<b>The Ethiopian Didascalia</b> (Didesqelya) — instructions to bishops and the people, related to the
Syriac <i>Didascalia of the Apostles</i> and the <i>Apostolic Constitutions</i>, but in its own recension.

<p class="footer-note">None of these eight books exists in a complete French translation; scholars access them through
scholarly editions of the Ge'ez or through partial English translations.</p>
